claim: The exosome complex mediates the degradation and processing of multiple classes of RNAs.
source: Since the highly conserved exosome complex mediates the degradation and processing of multiple classes of RNAs, it almost certainly controls diverse biological processes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Exosome complex subunits confer an erythroid maturation barricade.
source: Previously, we demonstrated that exosome complex subunits confer an erythroid maturation barricade, and the erythroid transcription factor GATA-1 dismantles the barricade by transcriptionally repressing the cognate genes.
evidence: This refers to previously published work by the authors (McIver et al., 2014).

claim: GATA-1 dismantles the erythroid maturation barricade by transcriptionally repressing genes encoding exosome complex subunits.
source: Previously, we demonstrated that exosome complex subunits confer an erythroid maturation barricade, and the erythroid transcription factor GATA-1 dismantles the barricade by transcriptionally repressing the cognate genes.
evidence: This refers to previously published work by the authors (McIver et al., 2014).

claim: The exosome complex ensures Kit receptor tyrosine kinase expression in erythroid precursor cells.
source: Exosome complex integrity in erythroid precursor cells ensures Kit receptor tyrosine kinase expression and stem cell factor/Kit signaling, while preventing responsiveness to erythropoietin-instigated signals that promote differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 7.

claim: The exosome complex ensures stem cell factor/Kit signaling in erythroid precursor cells.
source: Exosome complex integrity in erythroid precursor cells ensures Kit receptor tyrosine kinase expression and stem cell factor/Kit signaling, while preventing responsiveness to erythropoietin-instigated signals that promote differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by phospho-flow cytometry data in Figure 4 showing SCF-induced signaling is lost upon Exosc8 knockdown.

claim: The exosome complex prevents responsiveness to erythropoietin-instigated signals that promote differentiation.
source: Exosome complex integrity in erythroid precursor cells ensures Kit receptor tyrosine kinase expression and stem cell factor/Kit signaling, while preventing responsiveness to erythropoietin-instigated signals that promote differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by phospho-flow cytometry data in Figure 4 showing precocious Epo signaling upon Exosc8 knockdown.

claim: The exosome complex controls the massive production of erythroid cells that ensures organismal survival in homeostatic and stress contexts.
source: Functioning as a gatekeeper of this developmental signaling transition, the exosome complex controls the massive production of erythroid cells that ensures organismal survival in homeostatic and stress contexts.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing the exosome complex regulates the proliferation/differentiation balance.

claim: The first exosome complex subunit was discovered from an analysis of mechanisms controlling yeast rRNA synthesis.
source: The first subunit was discovered from an analysis of mechanisms controlling yeast rRNA synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mitchell et al., 1996.

claim: Mutations of Exosc2 (Rrp4) disrupt 5.8S rRNA 3'-end processing.
source: Mutations of Exosc2 (Rrp4) disrupt 5.8S rRNA 3'-end processing (Mitchell et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mitchell et al., 1996.

claim: Exosc2 assembles into a complex with components homologous to bacterial 3' to 5' exoribonuclease (PNPase).
source: Exosc2 assembles into a complex with components homologous to bacterial 3' to 5' exoribonuclease (PNPase) (Mitchell et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mitchell et al., 1997.

claim: Nine exosome complex subunits form a cylindrical core consisting of RNA binding subunits Exosc1, Exosc2 and Exosc3, which cap a ring formed by Exosc4, Exosc5, Exosc6, Exosc7, Exosc8 and Exosc9.
source: Nine exosome complex subunits form a cylindrical core consisting of the RNA binding subunits Exosc1 (Csl4), Exosc2 (Rrp4) and Exosc3 (Rrp40), which cap a ring formed by Exosc4 (Rrp41), Exosc5 (Rrp46), Exosc6 (Mtr3), Exosc7 (Rrp42), Exosc8 (Rrp43) and Exosc9 (Rrp45) (Liu et al., 2006; Makino et al., 2013; Makino et al., 2015; Wasmuth et al., 2014) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The vertebrate exosome complex core subunits lack RNA-degrading activity.
source: Despite homology with bacterial PNPases, the vertebrate core subunits lack RNA-degrading activity (Liu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2006.

claim: Dis3 (nuclear) and Dis3L (cytoplasmic) catalytic subunits bind the same position of the core complex, adjacent to Exosc4 and Exosc7.
source: Whereas Dis3 (Rrp44) (nuclear) and Dis3L (cytoplasmic) catalytic subunits bind the same position of the core complex, adjacent to Exosc4 and Exosc7, the predominantly nuclear catalytic subunit Exosc10 (Rrp6) binds the opposite site (Dziembowski et al., 2007; Makino et al., 2015) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The predominantly nuclear catalytic subunit Exosc10 (Rrp6) binds the opposite site from Dis3 and Dis3L.
source: Whereas Dis3 (Rrp44) (nuclear) and Dis3L (cytoplasmic) catalytic subunits bind the same position of the core complex, adjacent to Exosc4 and Exosc7, the predominantly nuclear catalytic subunit Exosc10 (Rrp6) binds the opposite site (Dziembowski et al., 2007; Makino et al., 2015) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The catalytic subunits of the exosome complex may function redundantly in certain contexts.
source: The catalytic subunits, which may function redundantly in certain contexts, mediate RNA degradation and/or processing (Kilchert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kilchert et al., 2016.

claim: Dis3L and Exosc10 are strictly exoribonucleases.
source: Unlike Dis3L and Exosc10, which are strictly exoribonucleases, Dis3 is also an endoribonuclease (Lebreton et al., 2008; Tomecki and Dziembowski, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lebreton et al., 2008 and Tomecki and Dziembowski, 2010.

claim: Dis3 is both an exoribonuclease and an endoribonuclease.
source: Unlike Dis3L and Exosc10, which are strictly exoribonucleases, Dis3 is also an endoribonuclease (Lebreton et al., 2008; Tomecki and Dziembowski, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lebreton et al., 2008 and Tomecki and Dziembowski, 2010.

claim: The core subunits of the exosome complex, except Exosc1, are considered to confer structural integrity.
source: The core subunits, except Exosc1, are considered to confer structural integrity (Liu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2006.

claim: Exosc8 knockdown in G1E-ER-GATA-1 cells reduces Exosc8 mRNA by approximately 75%.
source: Whereas knocking down Exosc8 or Exosc9 by ~75% (Figure 1B) did not alter Exosc2 levels in the input, the knockdowns reduced the amount of Exosc2 recovered with the anti-Exosc3 antibody (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with qRT-PCR data.

claim: Exosc9 knockdown in G1E-ER-GATA-1 cells reduces Exosc9 mRNA by approximately 75%.
source: Whereas knocking down Exosc8 or Exosc9 by ~75% (Figure 1B) did not alter Exosc2 levels in the input, the knockdowns reduced the amount of Exosc2 recovered with the anti-Exosc3 antibody (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with qRT-PCR data.

claim: Exosc8 knockdown does not alter Exosc2 protein levels in the input.
source: Whereas knocking down Exosc8 or Exosc9 by ~75% (Figure 1B) did not alter Exosc2 levels in the input, the knockdowns reduced the amount of Exosc2 recovered with the anti-Exosc3 antibody (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with Western blot data.

claim: Exosc9 knockdown does not alter Exosc2 protein levels in the input.
source: Whereas knocking down Exosc8 or Exosc9 by ~75% (Figure 1B) did not alter Exosc2 levels in the input, the knockdowns reduced the amount of Exosc2 recovered with the anti-Exosc3 antibody (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with Western blot data.

claim: Exosc8 knockdown reduces the amount of Exosc2 co-immunoprecipitated with Exosc3 by 58%.
source: Densitometric analysis indicated that Exosc8 and Exosc9 knockdowns reduced the amount of Exosc2 co-immunoprecipitated with Exosc3 by 58 (p=0.007) and 87% (p=1.3 × 10–4), respectively (Figure 1C, right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with densitometric analysis of co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Exosc9 knockdown reduces the amount of Exosc2 co-immunoprecipitated with Exosc3 by 87%.
source: Densitometric analysis indicated that Exosc8 and Exosc9 knockdowns reduced the amount of Exosc2 co-immunoprecipitated with Exosc3 by 58 (p=0.007) and 87% (p=1.3 × 10–4), respectively (Figure 1C, right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with densitometric analysis of co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Yeast Exosc8 (Rrp43) mutations decrease exosome complex stability and RNA binding.
source: Of relevance to this result, yeast Exosc8 (Rrp43) mutations decrease exosome complex stability and RNA binding (Lourenco et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lourenco et al., 2013.

claim: Exosc8 or Exosc9 downregulation disrupts Exosc3-Exosc2 interactions that only occur in the exosome complex.
source: As Exosc8 or Exosc9 downregulation disrupted Exosc3-Exosc2 interactions that only occur in the complex, erythroid maturation resulting from downregulating either of these subunits is associated with dismantling or destabilizing intra-complex protein-protein interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 1C.

claim: Erythroid maturation resulting from downregulating Exosc8 or Exosc9 is associated with dismantling or destabilizing intra-complex protein-protein interactions.
source: As Exosc8 or Exosc9 downregulation disrupted Exosc3-Exosc2 interactions that only occur in the complex, erythroid maturation resulting from downregulating either of these subunits is associated with dismantling or destabilizing intra-complex protein-protein interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 1C combined with previous maturation data.

claim: SCF/Kit signaling supports hematopoietic stem/progenitor cell and erythroid precursor cell proliferation and survival.
source: Whereas SCF/Kit signaling supports hematopoietic stem/progenitor cell (HSPC) and erythroid precursor cell proliferation and survival (Lennartsson and Ronnstrand, 2012), erythropoietin (Epo)/Epo receptor signaling uniquely promotes terminal differentiation (Munugalavadla and Kapur, 2005; Wu et al., 1995b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lennartsson and Ronnstrand, 2012.

claim: Erythropoietin (Epo)/Epo receptor signaling uniquely promotes terminal differentiation.
source: Whereas SCF/Kit signaling supports hematopoietic stem/progenitor cell (HSPC) and erythroid precursor cell proliferation and survival (Lennartsson and Ronnstrand, 2012), erythropoietin (Epo)/Epo receptor signaling uniquely promotes terminal differentiation (Munugalavadla and Kapur, 2005; Wu et al., 1995b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Munugalavadla and Kapur, 2005 and Wu et al., 1995b.

claim: Epo and SCF/Kit can synergistically promote proliferation and survival.
source: Epo and SCF/Kit can synergistically promote proliferation and survival (Joneja et al., 1997; Muta et al., 1994; Sui et al., 1998; Wu et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Without exogenous Epo, Exosc8 knockdown decreases live cells from 66% to 24%.
source: Without exogenous Epo, live cells decreased from 66 to 24% (control versus knockdown cells) (p=2 × 10–5), and late apoptotic cells increased proportionally (24 to 67%, p=3 × 10–4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and 2B with flow cytometry data.

claim: Without exogenous Epo, Exosc8 knockdown increases late apoptotic cells from 24% to 67%.
source: Without exogenous Epo, live cells decreased from 66 to 24% (control versus knockdown cells) (p=2 × 10–5), and late apoptotic cells increased proportionally (24 to 67%, p=3 × 10–4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and 2B with flow cytometry data.

claim: Exosc8 downregulation increases late apoptosis two-fold when cells are cultured in media containing 0.001 U/ml Epo.
source: Exosc8 downregulation increased late apoptosis two-fold (p=0.02) when cells were cultured in media containing 0.001 U/ml Epo.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and 2B with flow cytometry data.

claim: Downregulating Exosc8 renders cell integrity hypersensitive to limiting concentrations of Epo.
source: Surprisingly, downregulating Exosc8 rendered cell integrity hypersensitive to limiting concentrations of Epo.
evidence: This is inferred from the apoptosis data in Figure 2.

claim: Exosc8 downregulation stimulates erythroid maturation (1.5 fold increase in R2 to R3 transition) in media containing 0.5 U/ml Epo.
source: Whereas Exosc8 downregulation stimulated erythroid maturation (1.5 fold increase in R2 to R3 transition, p=0.003) in media containing 0.5 U/ml Epo, maturation of Exosc8-knockdown cells did not proceed without exogenous Epo (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and 3B with flow cytometry data.

claim: Maturation of Exosc8-knockdown cells does not proceed without exogenous Epo.
source: Whereas Exosc8 downregulation stimulated erythroid maturation (1.5 fold increase in R2 to R3 transition, p=0.003) in media containing 0.5 U/ml Epo, maturation of Exosc8-knockdown cells did not proceed without exogenous Epo (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and 3B with flow cytometry data.

claim: Without Epo, Exosc8 downregulation increases the percentage of immature erythroid precursors (R1).
source: Without Epo, Exosc8 downregulation also increased the percentage of immature erythroid precursors (R1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and 3B with flow cytometry data.

claim: Exosc8 downregulation increases orthochromatic erythroblasts (gate IV) 8 fold.
source: Orthochromatic erythroblasts (gate IV) increased 8 fold (p=0.006) or seven fold (p=3.5 × 10–5) post-Exosc8 or -Exosc9 downregulation, respectively.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 with flow cytometry data.

claim: Exosc9 downregulation increases orthochromatic erythroblasts (gate IV) 7 fold.
source: Orthochromatic erythroblasts (gate IV) increased 8 fold (p=0.006) or seven fold (p=3.5 × 10–5) post-Exosc8 or -Exosc9 downregulation, respectively.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 with flow cytometry data.

claim: Exosc8 downregulation increases erythrocytes (gate VI) two fold.
source: Erythrocytes (gate VI) increased two fold (Exosc8, p=0.005, Exosc9, p=0.005).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 with flow cytometry data.

claim: Exosc9 downregulation increases erythrocytes (gate VI) two fold.
source: Erythrocytes (gate VI) increased two fold (Exosc8, p=0.005, Exosc9, p=0.005).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 with flow cytometry data.

claim: Exosc8 downregulation reduces the number of early SCF, IL-3 and Epo-dependent BFU-E colonies by 10 fold.
source: Exosc8 downregulation reduced the number of early SCF, IL-3 and Epo-dependent BFU-E (Burst Forming Unit – Erythroid) colonies by 10 fold (p=4.7 × 10–10).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D with colony assay data.

claim: Exosc8 downregulation does not affect the number of Epo dependent CFU-E colonies.
source: However, the number of Epo dependent CFU-E (Colony Forming Unit – Erythroid) colonies was unaffected (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D with colony assay data.

claim: SCF induces maximal Akt phosphorylation in immature erythroblasts (Ter119-/CD71high) at 5.5 fold.
source: SCF induced maximal Akt phosphorylation in immature erythroblasts (Ter119-/CD71high) (5.5 fold, p=3 × 10–6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B with phospho-flow cytometry data.

claim: As erythroid maturation progresses to Ter119+/CD71high and Ter119+/CD71low stages, the SCF response is diminished.
source: As erythroid maturation progressed to Ter119+/CD71high and Ter119+/CD71low stages, the SCF response was diminished (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B with phospho-flow cytometry data.

claim: Exosc8 downregulation abrogates SCF-mediated induction of phospho-Akt.
source: Exosc8 downregulation abrogated SCF-mediated induction of phospho-Akt (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B with phospho-flow cytometry data.

claim: Epo induces maximal Akt phosphorylation in Ter119+/CD71high erythroblasts.
source: Epo induced maximal Akt phosphorylation in Ter119+/CD71high erythroblasts, and Exosc8 downregulation accelerated acquisition of this signaling response.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C with phospho-flow cytometry data.

claim: Exosc8 downregulation accelerates acquisition of Epo-induced Akt phosphorylation.
source: Epo induced maximal Akt phosphorylation in Ter119+/CD71high erythroblasts, and Exosc8 downregulation accelerated acquisition of this signaling response.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C with phospho-flow cytometry data.

claim: Epo does not affect Akt phosphorylation in control Ter119-/CD71high erythroblasts.
source: Whereas Epo did not affect Akt phosphorylation in control Ter119-/CD71high erythroblasts, Epo increased phospho-Akt 4 fold (p=0.003) in Exosc8-knockdown Ter119-/CD71high erythroblasts (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C with phospho-flow cytometry data.

claim: Epo increases phospho-Akt 4 fold in Exosc8-knockdown Ter119-/CD71high erythroblasts.
source: Whereas Epo did not affect Akt phosphorylation in control Ter119-/CD71high erythroblasts, Epo increased phospho-Akt 4 fold (p=0.003) in Exosc8-knockdown Ter119-/CD71high erythroblasts (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C with phospho-flow cytometry data.

claim: Downregulating an exosome complex subunit abrogates SCF signaling that supports precursor proliferation/amplification.
source: Thus, downregulating an exosome complex subunit that dismantles intra-complex protein-protein interactions abrogates SCF signaling that supports precursor proliferation/amplification, while precociously inducing pro-differentiation Epo signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the phospho-flow cytometry data in Figure 4.

claim: Downregulating an exosome complex subunit precociously induces pro-differentiation Epo signaling.
source: Thus, downregulating an exosome complex subunit that dismantles intra-complex protein-protein interactions abrogates SCF signaling that supports precursor proliferation/amplification, while precociously inducing pro-differentiation Epo signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the phospho-flow cytometry data in Figure 4.

claim: The exosome complex orchestrates a developmental signaling transition that dictates whether erythroid precursors undergo sustained proliferation or differentiate.
source: By orchestrating this developmental signaling transition, the exosome complex ensures a balance between proliferation/amplification and differentiation - a balance that shifts physiologically towards differentiation as GATA-1 represses genes encoding exosome complex subunits (McIver et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the signaling data in Figure 4 and previous work.

claim: R2 erythroblasts express the highest levels of cell surface Kit.
source: Using flow cytometry with primary fetal liver erythroblasts, R2 erythroblasts expressed the highest levels of cell surface Kit, and Exosc8 downregulation reduced cell surface Kit to a nearly undetectable level (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A with flow cytometry data.

claim: Exosc8 downregulation reduces cell surface Kit to a nearly undetectable level.
source: Using flow cytometry with primary fetal liver erythroblasts, R2 erythroblasts expressed the highest levels of cell surface Kit, and Exosc8 downregulation reduced cell surface Kit to a nearly undetectable level (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A with flow cytometry data.

claim: Exosc9 downregulation reduces cell surface Kit 6 fold in R2 cells.
source: Similarly, Exosc9 downregulation reduced cell surface Kit 6 fold in R2 cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B with flow cytometry data.

claim: Exosc8 downregulation reduces Kit mRNA and primary transcript levels at all stages of erythroid maturation.
source: Exosc8 downregulation reduced Kit mRNA and primary transcript levels at all stages of erythroid maturation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C with qRT-PCR data.

claim: By 24 hr post-infection with shExosc8-expressing retrovirus, total Kit protein declines 10 fold in Ter119- erythroid precursor cells.
source: By 24 hr post-infection with shExosc8-expressing retrovirus, total Kit protein declined 10 fold (p=0.046) in Ter119- erythroid precursor cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C with Western blot data.

claim: Exosc8 downregulation modestly increases Gata2 mRNA in R3 cells.
source: Exosc8 downregulation modestly increased Gata2 mRNA in R3 cells, but GATA-2 protein levels were not significantly affected in Ter119- cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D with qRT-PCR and Western blot data.

claim: GATA-2 protein levels are not significantly affected by Exosc8 downregulation in Ter119- cells.
source: Exosc8 downregulation modestly increased Gata2 mRNA in R3 cells, but GATA-2 protein levels were not significantly affected in Ter119- cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D with Western blot data.

claim: GATA-1 increases slightly (1.4 fold) in Exosc8-knockdown Ter119- cells.
source: GATA-1 increased slightly in Exosc8-knockdown Ter119- cells (1.4 fold, p=0.02) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D with Western blot data.

claim: Downregulating Exosc8 has little to no effect on Samd14 expression.
source: Downregulating Exosc8 had little to no effect on Samd14 expression (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D with qRT-PCR data.

claim: Downregulating Exosc8 does not affect the maturation-dependent reduction in Vim or Hdc mRNA levels.
source: Downregulating Exosc8 did not affect the maturation-dependent reduction in Vim or Hdc mRNA levels (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D with qRT-PCR data.

claim: At 24 hr post-infection with shExosc8-expressing retrovirus, Exosc8 mRNA declines by 70%.
source: At 24 hr post-infection of fetal liver erythroid precursor cells with shRNA-expressing retrovirus, Exosc8 mRNA declined by 70% (p=0.005).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E with qRT-PCR data.

claim: At 24 hr post-infection with shExosc8-expressing retrovirus, Kit mRNA decreases by 46%.
source: Whereas Kit mRNA decreased by 46% (p=0.002), expression of the GATA-1/Exosc8-regulated cell cycle-regulatory genes Cdkn1b (p27Kip1), Ddit3, Gadd45a, Gas2l1 and Trp53inp1 was not significantly altered (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E with qRT-PCR data.

claim: At 24 hr post-infection with shExosc8-expressing retrovirus, expression of GATA-1/Exosc8-regulated cell cycle-regulatory genes Cdkn1b, Ddit3, Gadd45a, Gas2l1 and Trp53inp1 is not significantly altered.
source: Whereas Kit mRNA decreased by 46% (p=0.002), expression of the GATA-1/Exosc8-regulated cell cycle-regulatory genes Cdkn1b (p27Kip1), Ddit3, Gadd45a, Gas2l1 and Trp53inp1 was not significantly altered (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E with qRT-PCR data.

claim: At 24 hr post-infection, there is only a slight increase in the percentage of G1 cells (30% in control and 33.5% in Exosc8-knockdown cells).
source: Analysis of the cell cycle status of Kit-expressing Ter119- erythroid precursor cells 24 and 72 hr post-infection revealed only a slight increase in the percentage of G1 cells at 24 hr (30% in control and 33.5% in Exosc8-knockdown cells (p=2 × 10–6)).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F with cell cycle analysis data.

claim: At 72 hr post-infection, 49.5% of Exosc8-knockdown Ter119- cells are in G1, in comparison with 36% of control cells.
source: At 72 hr post-infection, 49.5% of Exosc8-knockdown Ter119- cells were in G1, in comparison with 36% of control cells (p=1.6 × 10–6) (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F with cell cycle analysis data.

claim: The prominent cell cycle arrest resulting from Exosc8 downregulation occurs after Kit is repressed.
source: Thus, the prominent cell cycle arrest resulting from Exosc8 downregulation occurs after Kit is repressed.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal analysis of Kit expression and cell cycle status in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: shRNA-mediated Exosc8 downregulation in GATA-1-null G1E cells reduces Kit mRNA by 37%.
source: shRNA-mediated Exosc8 downregulation in GATA-1-null G1E proerythroblast-like cells reduced Kit mRNA by 37% (p=0.002) (Figure 5G), and Kit cell surface expression by 44% in the GFP+ population (p=3.3 × 10–8).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5G with qRT-PCR data.

claim: shRNA-mediated Exosc8 downregulation in GATA-1-null G1E cells reduces Kit cell surface expression by 44% in the GFP+ population.
source: shRNA-mediated Exosc8 downregulation in GATA-1-null G1E proerythroblast-like cells reduced Kit mRNA by 37% (p=0.002) (Figure 5G), and Kit cell surface expression by 44% in the GFP+ population (p=3.3 × 10–8).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5H with flow cytometry data.

claim: Cell surface Kit is unaffected in the GFP- population of G1E cells after Exosc8 downregulation.
source: Importantly, cell surface Kit was unaffected in the GFP- population (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5H with flow cytometry data.

claim: Exosome complex disruption downregulates Kit expression independent of alterations in cell cycle status.
source: In aggregate, these analyses support a model in which exosome complex disruption downregulates Kit expression independent of alterations in cell cycle status and is not a consequence of cell cycle arrest or cellular maturation.
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figures 5E-H showing Kit downregulation precedes cell cycle arrest and occurs in non-differentiating G1E cells.

claim: Exosome complex disruption downregulates Kit expression independent of cellular maturation.
source: In aggregate, these analyses support a model in which exosome complex disruption downregulates Kit expression independent of alterations in cell cycle status and is not a consequence of cell cycle arrest or cellular maturation.
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figures 5E-H showing Kit downregulation occurs in non-differentiating G1E cells.

claim: Kit expression is 5.9 fold lower in Exosc3-/- ES cells versus control cells.
source: Consistent with these results, mining RNA-seq data from normal and Exosc3-/- ES cells (Pefanis et al., 2015) revealed Kit expression 5.9 fold lower in mutant versus control cells (transcripts per million, false discovery rate < 0.05).
evidence: This is based on analysis of published RNA-seq data from Pefanis et al., 2015.

claim: Exosc8 downregulation reduces phospho-Ser5 Pol II occupancy within the Kit coding region (+5 kb) and 3' UTR.
source: Using quantitative ChIP analysis with control and Exosc8-knockdown Ter119- cells, Exosc8 downregulation reduced phospho-Ser5 Pol II occupancy within the coding region (+5 kb) and 3' UTR, but not at the promoter (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A with ChIP data.

claim: Exosc8 downregulation does not alter phospho-Ser5 Pol II occupancy at the Kit promoter.
source: Using quantitative ChIP analysis with control and Exosc8-knockdown Ter119- cells, Exosc8 downregulation reduced phospho-Ser5 Pol II occupancy within the coding region (+5 kb) and 3' UTR, but not at the promoter (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A with ChIP data.

claim: Exosc8 downregulation does not alter phospho-Ser5 Pol II occupancy at the active Rpb1 gene or the inactive Krt5 gene.
source: Exosc8 downregulation did not alter phospho-Ser5 Pol II occupancy at the active Rpb1 gene or the inactive Krt5 gene (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A with ChIP data.

claim: Exosc8 downregulation does not influence GATA-1 occupancy at Kit at -114, +5 and +58 kb sites.
source: Exosc8 downregulation did not influence GATA-1 occupancy at -114, +5 and +58 kb sites, relative to the promoter (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A with ChIP data.

claim: Endogenous Exosc9 occupies the Kit promoter, the coding region and the 3'-UTR.
source: Quantitative ChIP analysis with fetal liver erythroid precursor cells expanded for 48 hr revealed endogenous Exosc9 occupancy at the Kit promoter, the coding region and the 3'-UTR, with occupancy higher at the promoter and coding region sites versus the 3'-UTR (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B with ChIP data.

claim: Exosc9 occupancy is higher at the Kit promoter and coding region sites versus the 3'-UTR.
source: Quantitative ChIP analysis with fetal liver erythroid precursor cells expanded for 48 hr revealed endogenous Exosc9 occupancy at the Kit promoter, the coding region and the 3'-UTR, with occupancy higher at the promoter and coding region sites versus the 3'-UTR (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B with ChIP data.

claim: Exosc9 occupies the Alas2, Slc4a1 and Hbb-b1 promoters.
source: Exosc9 also occupied the Alas2, Slc4a1 and Hbb-b1 promoters, with less occupancy at the MyoD promoter (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B with ChIP data.

claim: Exosc9 has less occupancy at the MyoD promoter compared to Alas2, Slc4a1 and Hbb-b1 promoters.
source: Exosc9 also occupied the Alas2, Slc4a1 and Hbb-b1 promoters, with less occupancy at the MyoD promoter (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B with ChIP data.

claim: Exosc9 occupancy implies that the exosome complex directly regulates transcription of Kit, Alas2, Slc4a1 and Hbb-b1 loci.
source: Exosc9 occupancy implies that the exosome complex directly regulates transcription of these loci.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP data in Figure 6B showing Exosc9 occupancy at these loci.

claim: At 48 hr post-infection, Exosc8 downregulation increases R3 cells from 35% to 63%.
source: By 48 hr, Exosc8 downregulation increased R3 cells from 35 to 63% (p=4 × 10–7), while reducing R2 cells two-fold (p=4 × 10–5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and 7B with flow cytometry data.

claim: At 48 hr post-infection, Exosc8 downregulation reduces R2 cells two-fold.
source: By 48 hr, Exosc8 downregulation increased R3 cells from 35 to 63% (p=4 × 10–7), while reducing R2 cells two-fold (p=4 × 10–5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and 7B with flow cytometry data.

claim: Kit expression prevents Exosc8 knockdown-dependent maturation, reducing R3 cells from 63% to 27%.
source: Kit expression prevented Exosc8 knockdown-dependent maturation, reducing R3 cells from 63 to 27% (p=1 × 10–7).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and 7B with flow cytometry data.

claim: Kit expression, concomitant with Exosc8 downregulation, rescues R2 cells (increased from 21% to 42%).
source: Kit expression, concomitant with Exosc8 downregulation, rescued R2 cells (increased from 21 to 42%, p=8 × 10–4) to a level indistinguishable from control cells (45%).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and 7B with flow cytometry data.

claim: At 48 hr, Kit expression in control cells increases R2 cells from 45% to 66%.
source: At 48 hr, Kit expression in control cells increased R2 cells from 45 to 66% (p=6 × 10–5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and 7B with flow cytometry data.

claim: At 72 hr, Exosc8-knockdown cells have 18% R4, 56% R3 and 17% R2 versus 2% R4, 41% R3, and 47% R2 for control cells.
source: At 72 hr, Exosc8-knockdown cells matured further (18% R4, 56% R3 and 17% R2 versus 2% R4 (p=4 × 10–5), 41% R3 (p=3 × 10–5), and 47% R2 (p=3 × 10–6) for control cells).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and 7B with flow cytometry data.

claim: At 72 hr, expressing Kit in Exosc8-knockdown cells reduces R4 from 18% to 7%, R3 from 56% to 28%, while increasing R2 from 17% to 38%.
source: Expressing Kit in Exosc8-knockdown cells reduced R4 from 18 to 7% (p=4 × 10–5), R3 from 56 to 28% (p=9 × 10–7), while increasing R2 from 17 to 38% (p=5 × 10–5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and 7B with flow cytometry data.

claim: At 72 hr, Kit expression increases R2 cells from 47% to 68%.
source: At 72 hr, Kit expression increased R2 cells from 47 to 68% (p=6 × 10–5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and 7B with flow cytometry data.

claim: Exosc8 downregulation reduces Kit MFI six fold.
source: Exosc8 downregulation reduced Kit MFI six fold (p=0.001).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C with flow cytometry data.

claim: 50 μl of Kit retroviral supernatant increases Kit cell surface expression in Exosc8-knockdown cells to approximately the endogenous level (1.2 fold higher than control).
source: At 48 hr post-infection, 50 μl of Kit retroviral supernatant (half of that used in the time-course) increased Kit cell surface expression in Exosc8-knockdown cells to approximately the endogenous level (1.2 fold higher than control).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C with flow cytometry data.

claim: Infection of control cells with Kit retrovirus increases Kit cell surface expression three fold.
source: Under these conditions, infection of control cells increased Kit cell surface expression three fold (p=0.002).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C with flow cytometry data.

claim: Exosc8 downregulation, without ectopic Kit expression, increases the percentage of R3 cells approximately two fold 48 hr post-infection.
source: Exosc8 downregulation, without ectopic Kit expression, increased the percentage of R3 cells ~two fold (p=0.003) 48 hr post-infection.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C with flow cytometry data.

claim: The increased R3 population induced by Exosc8 downregulation is prevented by enforced Kit expression at 1.2 fold higher than the endogenous level.
source: The increased R3 population cells induced by Exosc8 downregulation was prevented by enforced Kit expression at 1.2 fold higher than the endogenous level (control R3, 19.7% versus Exosc8/Kit R3, 16.5%).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C with flow cytometry data.

claim: A three fold increase in Kit cell surface expression in the control condition decreases the R3 population from 19.7% to 6%.
source: A three fold increase in Kit cell surface expression in the control condition decreased the R3 population cells from 19.7% to 6% (p=0.001) (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C with flow cytometry data.

claim: Enforced Kit expression negates erythroid maturation induced by exosome complex disruption.
source: As enforced Kit expression negated erythroid maturation induced by exosome complex disruption, the exosome complex activity to establish and/or maintain Kit expression is a critical step in the exosome complex-dependent maturation process.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments in Figure 7.

claim: The exosome complex activity to establish and/or maintain Kit expression is a critical step in the exosome complex-dependent maturation process.
source: As enforced Kit expression negated erythroid maturation induced by exosome complex disruption, the exosome complex activity to establish and/or maintain Kit expression is a critical step in the exosome complex-dependent maturation process.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments in Figure 7.

claim: Wnt signaling promotes intestinal stem cell self-renewal.
source: Wnt signaling promotes intestinal stem cell self-renewal, while Bone Morphogenetic Protein (BMP) signaling suppresses self-renewal and promotes differentiation (Clevers et al., 2014; He et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Clevers et al., 2014 and He et al., 2004.

claim: Bone Morphogenetic Protein (BMP) signaling suppresses intestinal stem cell self-renewal and promotes differentiation.
source: Wnt signaling promotes intestinal stem cell self-renewal, while Bone Morphogenetic Protein (BMP) signaling suppresses self-renewal and promotes differentiation (Clevers et al., 2014; He et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Clevers et al., 2014 and He et al., 2004.

claim: SCF signaling promotes erythroid precursor cell proliferation at the expense of differentiation.
source: In hematopoiesis, SCF signaling promotes erythroid precursor cell proliferation at the expense of differentiation (Haas et al., 2015; Muta et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Haas et al., 2015 and Muta et al., 1995.

claim: During stress erythropoiesis, Epo, SCF and glucocorticoids synergistically promote erythroid cell expansion.
source: During stress erythropoiesis, Epo, SCF and glucocorticoids synergistically promote erythroid cell expansion (Kolbus et al., 2003; Wessely et al., 1997) and Kit downregulation promotes maturation (Haas et al., 2015; Munugalavadla et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kolbus et al., 2003 and Wessely et al., 1997.

claim: Kit downregulation promotes erythroid maturation.
source: During stress erythropoiesis, Epo, SCF and glucocorticoids synergistically promote erythroid cell expansion (Kolbus et al., 2003; Wessely et al., 1997) and Kit downregulation promotes maturation (Haas et al., 2015; Munugalavadla et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Haas et al., 2015 and Munugalavadla et al., 2005.

claim: Kit signaling induces Epo receptor tyrosine phosphorylation.
source: Kit signaling induces Epo receptor tyrosine phosphorylation (Wu et al., 1995a), although synergistic enhancement of proliferation may involve convergence of SCF and Epo signals on ERK1/2 via distinct pathways (Sui et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wu et al., 1995a.

claim: Synergistic enhancement of proliferation by SCF and Epo may involve convergence of signals on ERK1/2 via distinct pathways.
source: Kit signaling induces Epo receptor tyrosine phosphorylation (Wu et al., 1995a), although synergistic enhancement of proliferation may involve convergence of SCF and Epo signals on ERK1/2 via distinct pathways (Sui et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sui et al., 1998.

claim: Constitutively active Kit inhibits Epo-mediated Akt phosphorylation, increasing apoptosis in mature erythroid cells.
source: Constitutively active Kit inhibits Epo-mediated Akt phosphorylation, increasing apoptosis in mature erythroid cells (Haas et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Haas et al., 2015.

claim: GATA-1 and Scl/TAL1 repress Kit transcription as erythroblasts acquire Epo-dependence.
source: GATA-1 and the cooperating transcription factor Scl/TAL1 repress Kit transcription as erythroblasts acquire Epo-dependence (Munugalavadla et al., 2005; Vitelli et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Munugalavadla et al., 2005 and Vitelli et al., 2000.

claim: The exosome complex establishes the proliferation/differentiation balance by ensuring expression of Kit under conditions in which progenitors are not competent to transduce Epo pro-differentiation signals.
source: The exosome complex establishes the balance by ensuring expression of a receptor tyrosine kinase, Kit, which is essential for proliferation, under conditions in which progenitors are not competent to transduce Epo pro-differentiation signals.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data in Figures 4, 5, and 7.

claim: Disrupting exosome complex integrity downregulates Kit and SCF-mediated proliferation signaling, while inducing Epo signaling.
source: Disrupting exosome complex integrity downregulated Kit and SCF-mediated proliferation signaling, while inducing Epo signaling (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: GATA-1 represses expression of exosome complex subunits, instigating the developmental signaling transition.
source: Physiologically, GATA-1 represses expression of exosome complex subunits, instigating the developmental signaling transition.
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited as McIver et al., 2014.

claim: Reduced SCF signaling upon exosome complex disruption would be predicted to underlie or contribute to activation of Epo signaling in erythroid precursor cells.
source: Reduced SCF signaling upon exosome complex disruption would be predicted to underlie or contribute to activation of Epo signaling in erythroid precursor cells (Figures 4, 5) and promote erythroid differentiation (Figures 3, 7).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings in Figures 3, 4, 5, and 7.

claim: An RNA-regulatory machine orchestrates the balance between opposing developmental signaling pathways.
source: Our results establish a paradigm in which an RNA-regulatory machine orchestrates the balance between opposing developmental signaling pathways.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on all experimental findings.

claim: The exosome complex paradigm may operate to control additional progenitor cell transitions.
source: Considering the apparent ubiquitous expression of the exosome complex, it is attractive to propose that the paradigm may operate to control additional progenitor cell transitions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings in erythroid cells.

claim: Mice homozygous for the W mutation (white spotting) in Kit die perinatally from severe macrocytic anemia.
source: Mice homozygous for the W mutation (white spotting) in Kit die perinatally from severe macrocytic anemia (Bernstein et al., 1990; Waskow et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bernstein et al., 1990 and Waskow et al., 2004.

claim: The anemia in W mutant mice likely reflects the Kit requirement for HSPC genesis, maintenance and function.
source: The anemia likely reflects the Kit requirement for HSPC genesis, maintenance and function (Bernstein et al., 1990; Ding et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bernstein et al., 1990 and Ding et al., 2012.

claim: The exosome complex is enriched at actively transcribed genes.
source: The exosome complex is enriched at actively transcribed genes (Andrulis et al., 2002; Lim et al., 2013), regulates transcription start site usage (Jenks et al., 2008; Kuehner and Brow, 2008), influences heterochromatin and post-transcriptional gene silencing (Eberle et al., 2015) and regulates superenhancer activity (Pefanis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Andrulis et al., 2002 and Lim et al., 2013.

claim: The exosome complex regulates transcription start site usage.
source: The exosome complex is enriched at actively transcribed genes (Andrulis et al., 2002; Lim et al., 2013), regulates transcription start site usage (Jenks et al., 2008; Kuehner and Brow, 2008), influences heterochromatin and post-transcriptional gene silencing (Eberle et al., 2015) and regulates superenhancer activity (Pefanis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jenks et al., 2008 and Kuehner and Brow, 2008.

claim: The exosome complex influences heterochromatin and post-transcriptional gene silencing.
source: The exosome complex is enriched at actively transcribed genes (Andrulis et al., 2002; Lim et al., 2013), regulates transcription start site usage (Jenks et al., 2008; Kuehner and Brow, 2008), influences heterochromatin and post-transcriptional gene silencing (Eberle et al., 2015) and regulates superenhancer activity (Pefanis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eberle et al., 2015.

claim: The exosome complex regulates superenhancer activity.
source: The exosome complex is enriched at actively transcribed genes (Andrulis et al., 2002; Lim et al., 2013), regulates transcription start site usage (Jenks et al., 2008; Kuehner and Brow, 2008), influences heterochromatin and post-transcriptional gene silencing (Eberle et al., 2015) and regulates superenhancer activity (Pefanis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pefanis et al., 2015.

claim: Gene promoters are bidirectional in nature.
source: Gene promoters are bidirectional in nature (Andersson et al., 2015), and the exosome complex rapidly degrades PROMPTs (Lubas et al., 2011; Preker et al., 2011; Preker et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Andersson et al., 2015.

claim: The exosome complex rapidly degrades PROMPTs (promoter upstream transcripts).
source: Gene promoters are bidirectional in nature (Andersson et al., 2015), and the exosome complex rapidly degrades PROMPTs (Lubas et al., 2011; Preker et al., 2011; Preker et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lubas et al., 2011, Preker et al., 2011, and Preker et al., 2008.

claim: Depletion of exosome complex components stabilizes PROMPTs and additional cryptic transcripts present at gene loci.
source: Depletion of exosome complex components stabilizes PROMPTs and additional cryptic transcripts present at gene loci, including PSARs (promoter-associated small RNAs), TSARs (terminator-associated small RNAs), PALRs (promoter-associated long RNAs), TSSa RNAs (transcription start site-associated RNAs) and eRNAs (enhancer RNAs) (Jensen et al., 2013; Lubas et al., 2015; Pefanis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jensen et al., 2013, Lubas et al., 2015, and Pefanis et al., 2015.

claim: Genes encoding exosome complex components are linked to cancer (DIS3).
source: Genes encoding exosome complex components are linked to pathologies including cancer (DIS3) (Chapman et al., 2011), immune disorders (EXOSC9 and EXOSC10) (Allmang et al., 1999b) and congenital neurological disorders (EXOSC3 and EXOSC8) (Boczonadi et al., 2014; Rudnik-Schoneborn et al., 2013; Wan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chapman et al., 2011.

claim: Genes encoding exosome complex components are linked to immune disorders (EXOSC9 and EXOSC10).
source: Genes encoding exosome complex components are linked to pathologies including cancer (DIS3) (Chapman et al., 2011), immune disorders (EXOSC9 and EXOSC10) (Allmang et al., 1999b) and congenital neurological disorders (EXOSC3 and EXOSC8) (Boczonadi et al., 2014; Rudnik-Schoneborn et al., 2013; Wan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Allmang et al., 1999b.

claim: Genes encoding exosome complex components are linked to congenital neurological disorders (EXOSC3 and EXOSC8).
source: Genes encoding exosome complex components are linked to pathologies including cancer (DIS3) (Chapman et al., 2011), immune disorders (EXOSC9 and EXOSC10) (Allmang et al., 1999b) and congenital neurological disorders (EXOSC3 and EXOSC8) (Boczonadi et al., 2014; Rudnik-Schoneborn et al., 2013; Wan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boczonadi et al., 2014, Rudnik-Schoneborn et al., 2013, and Wan et al., 2012.

claim: Downregulating EXOSC10, EXOSC9 or EXOSC7 expression causes differentiation of human epidermal progenitor cells.
source: Downregulating EXOSC10, EXOSC9 or EXOSC7 expression caused differentiation of human epididymal progenitor cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mistry et al., 2012.

claim: The exosome complex represses GRHL3, a key transcription factor promoting epidermal differentiation.
source: Mechanistically, the exosome complex represses GRHL3, a key transcription factor promoting epidermal differentiation (Mistry et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mistry et al., 2012.

claim: Exosc3 downregulation increases the R4 (late basophilic/orthochromatic erythroblasts) cell population nine fold.
source: In particular, Exosc3 downregulation using two distinct shRNAs increased the R4 (late basophilic/orthochromatic erythroblasts) cell population nine fold (p=0.006 and p=0.01 for the two shRNAs, respectively) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 with flow cytometry data.
